planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Confucius was raised at the Kunming Botanical Institute in Yunnan from a cross of Camellia reticulata and C. pitardii var. yunnanica and registered in the 1950s.

directions: Confucius was bred at the Kunming Botanical Institute in Yunnan, China from a cross of Camellia reticulata and the closely related C. pitardii var. yunnanica, and has been grown and traded internationally since the mid-twentieth century. Its large, orchid-pink, semi-double flowers have a high center of intermingled stamens and petaloids, a looser and more informal look than many pure reticulata selections. Plant in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in dappled shade, sheltered from strong wind, since the large flowers and broad leaves are easily damaged in an exposed site. Feed lightly after flowering and prune only to shape at that time, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's new growth.

common_name: Terrell Weaver Camellia (Large Red Reticulata-Japonica Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Terrell Weaver was bred in Macon, Georgia from reticulata 'Crimson Robe' crossed with japonica 'Ville de Nantes' and has been a popular Southern reticulata hybrid since the 1970s.

directions: Terrell Weaver was raised by camellia breeder Walter Homeyer of Macon, Georgia from a cross of Camellia reticulata 'Crimson Robe' and C. japonica 'Ville de Nantes,' combining reticulata-scale blooms with somewhat better cold tolerance from its japonica parent. Its large, deep red flowers open semi-double to loose peony form on a vigorous, upright shrub. Grow in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in filtered light, with protection from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind. Water deeply during dry spells and prune lightly right after bloom to shape, since flower buds for the next season form on new growth produced soon after flowering ends.

common_name: Tali Queen Camellia (Historic Deep Pink Yunnan Reticulata, Dali Cha)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tali Queen (Dali Cha) is a centuries-old Yunnan temple cultivar brought to the United States in 1948 along with the first wave of reticulata imports.

directions: Tali Queen, known in China as Dali Cha, is a historic Yunnan reticulata selection believed to be several hundred years old, brought to the United States in 1948 along with other early reticulata introductions. Its large, semi-double flowers have heavily textured, irregular outer petals in turkey red to deep pink surrounding a loose cluster of golden-anthered stamens. The plant is more tender and more sensitive to drought than many reticulata cultivars, so give it reliably moist, fast-draining, acidic soil and filtered shade with shelter from wind. Water deeply through dry spells, never letting the root zone dry out completely, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape, since next year's buds set on the current season's new growth.

common_name: Gunrei Azalea (Ruffled White Pink-Flecked Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Gunrei is a slow-growing, compact Satsuki azalea long favored for bonsai as well as container and border planting.

directions: Gunrei is a Satsuki azalea prized for its frilled, wide, overlapping white petals flecked and margined with light pink, with individual plants sometimes showing sectored or striped flowers alongside pure white or pink ones. Growth is slow and dense, making it a popular subject for bonsai training as well as small garden beds and containers. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since Satsuki azaleas are more shade-tolerant and more heat-tolerant than Kurume or Southern Indica types. Water regularly to keep the shallow roots from drying out, and prune only right after the late-spring to early-summer bloom, since this late-flowering group sets next year's buds soon after flowering ends.

common_name: Kazan Azalea (Ultra-Dwarf Reddish-Pink Satsuki Bonsai Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kazan is a dwarf sport of the Satsuki cultivar 'Taihai,' among the most compact and slowest-growing of all Satsuki selections.

directions: Kazan is an ultra-dwarf Satsuki azalea, a sport of the cultivar 'Taihai,' grown as much for its tiny, glossy, tear-drop-shaped leaves and tight mounding habit as for its small reddish-pink flowers in late spring. It is among the slowest-growing and most compact of all Satsuki selections, rarely exceeding two feet across after many years, which has made it a favorite subject for shohin bonsai. Grow in humus-rich, acidic, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, protected from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the fine foliage. Water attentively, since the dense, shallow root mass dries quickly, and prune or pinch only right after flowering to preserve the compact form.

common_name: Shugetsu Azalea (Autumn Moon, Bicolor Purple-and-White Satsuki Sport of Aikoku)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Shugetsu, sold in the U.S. nursery trade as Autumn Moon Azalea, is a sport of the Satsuki cultivar 'Aikoku.'

directions: Shugetsu, widely sold in the United States under the trade name Autumn Moon Azalea, is a sport of the older Satsuki cultivar 'Aikoku' and bears large, single, rounded flowers in deep purplish pink with a white center and throat, often edged or flecked in a bold bicolor pattern. Growth is upright and slower than Kurume or Southern Indica types, reaching roughly three feet tall over many years. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since Satsuki selections tolerate more shade and summer heat than earlier-blooming azalea groups. Water during dry spells to keep the shallow root zone evenly moist, and prune right after the late-spring to early-summer bloom, since flower buds for the following year set soon afterward.

common_name: Addy Wery Azalea (Vivid Vermilion-Orange Kurume Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Addy Wery was registered in the Netherlands in 1940 from a cross of Kurume parents 'Suetsumu' and 'Malvaticum.'

directions: Addy Wery is a compact Kurume azalea bred in the Netherlands in 1940 from a cross of 'Suetsumu' and 'Malvaticum,' prized for its small, funnel-shaped, intensely vermilion-to-orange-red flowers produced in such profusion that the small, dark-green foliage is nearly hidden in peak bloom. It forms a dense, rounded shrub that tolerates more open, sunnier sites than many evergreen azaleas, provided the soil stays consistently moist. Plant in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in cooler climates, sheltered from drying winter wind. Water deeply during dry spells and prune right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds form soon after the spring bloom ends.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Hatsugiri is a classic Kurume azalea introduced to the West from Japan around 1915, grown for its extremely heavy spring flower display.

directions: Hatsugiri is a low, wide-spreading Kurume azalea introduced from Japan to the West around 1915, grown for its abundant small, funnel-shaped, bright magenta-purple flowers that can cover the plant so thickly the foliage briefly disappears. The dense, mounding habit spreads wider than tall, making it useful as a low foundation or border shrub. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with shelter from harsh winter wind, since the evergreen foliage can brown in exposed sites. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while the plant is establishing, and prune lightly right after bloom, since flower buds for next spring set on new growth soon after flowering ends.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Amoena is one of the oldest Kurume-group azaleas grown in the West, introduced from Japan in the 1850s, predating E.H. Wilson's later 'Wilson's Fifty' introductions.

directions: Amoena is one of the oldest Kurume-group azaleas in Western cultivation, brought from Japan in the 1850s, well before E.H. Wilson's better-known 1918 introductions. Its small, funnel-shaped, vivid magenta-crimson flowers appear in such quantity in early to mid-spring that the small, dark evergreen leaves are nearly obscured. The upright, spreading shrub has proven reliable in European and American gardens for well over a century. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from strong winter wind. Water deeply during dry periods and prune only right after bloom, since flower buds for the following season set on new growth soon after flowering ends.

common_name: Tradition Azalea (Early-Blooming Cold-Hardy Deep Pink Kurume Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tradition is a Kurume azalea brought from Japan over a century ago and noted among Kurume selections for its cold hardiness.

directions: Tradition is a compact Kurume azalea brought from Japan to the United States over a century ago, valued for flowering unusually early in spring and for tolerating colder winters than many evergreen azaleas. It bears masses of small, deep pink, trumpet-shaped flowers on a slow-growing, low, rounded plant well suited to foundation plantings, borders, and containers. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled sun, sheltered from harsh winter wind in its coldest zones. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering, since flower buds for the next season set soon after the spring bloom ends.

common_name: Red Formosa Azalea (Deep Fuchsia-Red Sport of Formosa)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Formosa is a naturally occurring branch sport of the classic Southern Indica cultivar 'Formosa,' widely sold in the nursery trade under this name.

directions: Red Formosa arose as a naturally occurring branch sport of the classic Southern Indica azalea 'Formosa' and has become a widely sold nursery item in its own right, valued for large, fuchsia-red flowers often lightly freckled with deeper red on the upper petal. Like its parent, it is a large, fast-growing, heavy-blooming evergreen shrub well suited to Deep South landscapes and heat. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune right after flowering if size control is needed, since this vigorous grower can quickly exceed small spaces.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

common_name: Mardi Gras Azalea (Bicolor White-and-Pink Southern Indica Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mardi Gras is a compact, slower-growing Southern Indica azalea grown for its bicolor white-and-deep-pink blooms.

directions: Mardi Gras is a Southern Indica azalea grown for its large, bicolor flowers, white with a deep pink center and throat, produced heavily in early to mid-spring. Compared to older Southern Indica standards like 'Formosa' and 'George Lindley Taber,' it stays somewhat lower and more compact, fitting more readily into foundation plantings and smaller Gulf Coast and Deep South gardens. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with some protection from the hottest afternoon sun. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while the plant is establishing, and prune right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for the next bloom cycle form on new growth soon after.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens
